parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: force per unit length; force per unit current; length / current perpendicular to field
markscheme_points.guidance: 1 mark for any two points, 2 marks for all three points.

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking what $B$ is meant to measure - it tells you how strong the magnetic effect is in terms of the force it can exert on something carrying current.

Hint 2: Recall the force $F = BIL\sin\theta$ case - for the definition you need the special case where the force is maximum, so what must be true about the angle between current and field, and how can you rearrange to get $B$ on its own?
parts.proper_answer: Magnetic flux density is the force per unit length per unit current on a current-carrying conductor placed perpendicular to the field, $B = F/IL$ when $I$ is normal to $B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link B to force on a wire**
Think of $B$ as a way to say how much push a magnetic field can give. You have seen $F = BIL\sin\theta$ for a wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$. So $B$ must involve force divided by current and length.

Step 2: **Add the perpendicular condition**
The force is largest when the wire is at $90^{\circ}$ to the field, where $\sin\theta = 1$. The definition uses this maximum case. So in words: $B$ is the force per unit length when the current is $1\text{ A}$, or force per unit current when length is $1\text{ m}$, with length perpendicular to the field.

Step 3: **Write the full definition**
$$B = \frac{F}{IL}$$ for $I$ perpendicular to $B$. Unit is tesla, $\text{T}$. That covers all three ideas: per unit length, per unit current, perpendicular.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State an expression, in terms of some or all of $m$, $Q$, $B$ and $v$, for the magnetic force $F$ that acts on the particle when it is at point Y.
hints: Hint 1: The particle is moving at right angles to the field into a region of flux density $B$. Think which of $m, Q, B, v$ should control the size of the magnetic push - does mass matter here?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the moving-charge force**
A charge $Q$ moving at speed $v$ at right angles to flux density $B$ feels a magnetic force proportional to all three. Mass $m$ affects later motion but not the force size.

Step 2: **Write the expression**
$$F = BQv$$ This is the maximum force because $v$ is perpendicular to $B$ at point Y.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 7.1, draw an arrow at point Y to indicate the direction of the force in (b)(i).

markscheme_points.text: arrow at Y pointing vertically upwards

hints: Hint 1: Use Fleming's left-hand rule at Y: point your fingers for motion to the right and field into the page, then check where your thumb points for a positive charge.
parts.proper_answer: Force at Y is vertically upwards, perpendicular to both $v$ and $B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Fleming's left-hand rule**
First finger = field into the page, second finger = velocity (conventional current) to the right for the $+Q$ charge. Your thumb then points upwards.

Step 2: **Draw the arrow**
At point Y draw a short arrow starting at Y pointing vertically upwards. It must be at $90^{\circ}$ to the incoming path.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: On Fig. 7.1, draw a line to show a possible path for the particle through the region of the magnetic field.
hints: Hint 1: Remember the magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity, so it cannot speed the particle up but it bends it - think what shape of path has constant bending force toward the centre.
parts.proper_answer: Path curves upwards in a circular arc inside the field region.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why it bends**
The upward force at Y gives upward deflection. As soon as $v$ turns upward, the force direction also turns to stay perpendicular to $v$, always pointing to the same side.

Step 2: **Sketch the path**
Draw a smooth curve starting horizontal at Y then bending upward, part of a circle. It stays inside the shaded region, curving away from Z.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Explain how an electric field can be used with the magnetic field to ensure that the particle in (b) now passes through point Z.

markscheme_points.text: electric field applied vertically downwards (may be shown on a labelled diagram)
electric force on particle in opposite direction to magnetic force (may be shown on a labelled diagram)
particle undeflected when magnitudes of electric and magnetic forces are equal

hints: Hint 1: To get from Y straight across to Z the upward magnetic bending must be cancelled - so what direction must a new force act in?
Hint 2: An electric field $E$ exerts $F = EQ$ along the field on a positive charge - which way should $E$ point to give a downward push on $+Q$?
Hint 3: For a perfectly straight horizontal path the net force must be zero - what does that tell you about the sizes of the electric and magnetic forces?
parts.proper_answer: Apply a uniform electric field vertically downwards. It exerts a downward electric force on the $+Q$ particle, opposite to the upward magnetic force. Adjust $E$ so the two forces are equal in magnitude, giving zero resultant force and straight motion from Y to Z.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Need an opposing force**
Magnetic force alone bends the particle up. To go straight Y to Z you need a downward force of the same type of size to cancel it. That can be provided by an electric field.

Step 2: **Choose field direction**
Electric force on positive charge is in the direction of $E$. Since you need a downward force to oppose the upward $BQv$ force, $E$ must point vertically downwards.

Step 3: **Balance for no deflection**
When magnitudes are equal, resultant force is zero and the particle continues in a straight line at constant $v$ through to Z. This is the velocity-selector principle.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Derive an expression for $v$ in terms of $B$ and the electric field strength $E$.
hints: Hint 1: Start from the balance condition in (c)(i) - write down the electric force magnitude in terms of $E$ and $Q$ and set it equal to the magnetic force from (b)(i).
Hint 2: Look at what cancels on both sides when you equate them, then rearrange to leave $v$ on its own in terms of $E$ and $B$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Equate the two forces**
For undeflected motion:
$$\text{electric force} = \text{magnetic force}$$
$$EQ = BQv$$

Step 2: **Solve for v**
Charge $Q$ cancels from both sides:
$$E = Bv$$
$$v = \frac{E}{B}$$ Only particles with this speed pass straight through to Z.
